claims.text: Group A strep causes about 5% to 15% of adult pharyngitis (key takeaway, intro, citable summary)
claims.quote: Experts estimate that group A strep, the most common bacterial cause, causes ... 5% to 15% of pharyngitis infections in adults

claims.text: Viruses are the most common cause of acute pharyngitis
claims.quote: Viruses are the most common cause of pharyngitis in all age groups.

claims.text: Clear viral symptoms (cough, runny nose, hoarseness, mouth ulcers, conjunctivitis) usually do not need strep testing
claims.quote: Patients with clear viral symptoms don't need testing for group A streptococcal bacteria. ... Patients with group A strep pharyngitis typically don't have cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers, or conjunctivitis.

claims.text: Without clear viral features, examination alone, a photograph or a score cannot reliably distinguish strep from viral pharyngitis; testing decides
claims.quote: Healthcare providers can't use clinical examination to differentiate viral and group A strep pharyngitis

claims.text: Sudden throat pain, fever, front-neck nodes and inflamed or coated tonsils can be compatible with strep; exudate can occur with strep
claims.quote: Sudden onset of sore throat ... Fever ... Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy ... Tonsillar hypertrophy with or without exudates

claims.text: A negative rapid antigen test in a typical adult does not routinely need backup culture; CDC advises culture after a negative RADT in children older than 3 years
claims.quote: Children older than 3 years: Healthcare providers should follow up a negative RADT with a throat culture. All other ages: Throat culture after a negative RADT isn't routinely indicated.

claims.text: RADT has high specificity but variable sensitivity; culture is the gold standard
claims.quote: RADTs have high specificity for group A strep bacteria but varying sensitivities when compared to throat culture. ... Throat culture is the gold standard diagnostic test.

claims.text: A positive RADT or culture in a compatible illness supports antibiotics, which shorten symptoms, reduce transmission and decrease complications
claims.quote: Patients, regardless of age, who have a positive RADT or throat culture need antibiotics. ... Shortens the duration of symptoms ... Reduces the likelihood of transmission to close contacts ... Decreases the development of complications

claims.text: Penicillin or amoxicillin is generally first-line; CDC lists 10-day oral regimens
claims.quote: Penicillin or amoxicillin is the antibiotic of choice to treat group A strep pharyngitis. ... Adolescents and adults: 250 mg 4 times daily or 500 mg twice daily, for 10 days

claims.text: CDC advises avoiding cephalexin and cefadroxil with immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity; allergy type changes options
claims.quote: However, avoid cephalexin and cefadroxil in patients with immediate type hypersensitivity to penicillin.

claims.text: Macrolide and clindamycin resistance varies
claims.quote: resistance to azithromycin, clarithromycin, and clindamycin is well known and varies geographically and temporally.

claims.text: Stay home until fever-free and at least 12 to 24 hours after starting an appropriate antibiotic
claims.quote: People with group A strep pharyngitis should stay home from work, school, or daycare until both of the following are met: They are afebrile ... At least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotic therapy

claims.text: Hand washing and covering coughs reduce spread at home
claims.quote: Good hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette can reduce the spread of group A strep bacteria.

claims.text: General framing statements (decision framework, test choice, video limits, which test you had) rest on CDC testing guidance
claims.quote: Healthcare providers can't use clinical examination to differentiate viral and group A strep pharyngitis
